transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to see me?

Hi. Thank you for seeing me. Honestly, what made me finally come in is that... well, I keep getting up during our long sales strategy meetings at work. I know I’m supposed to just stay seated with everyone else, but I keep finding excuses to leave my chair, even if it’s just to go refill my water or pace by the printer for a bit. It's just been bothering me lately, so I figured I should talk to someone about it.
How long has this difficulty staying seated during meetings been going on? Has this been happening for years, or is this something more recent?
It's more recent, actually. I'd say it's really been noticeably affecting me since I changed into advertising sales strategy... that was about two years and two months ago.
Before you changed jobs two years ago, did you ever have trouble sitting still in meetings or other situations where you needed to stay seated for long periods?

Well, I guess if I really think about it, I've had trouble with this kind of thing for a long time. Like, way before high school, even. I remember my elementary school teachers always writing notes on my report cards saying I was bright but that I rushed through my work. They said I talked out of turn a lot, forgot my homework, and my desk was just... always stuffed with half-finished papers. So, yeah, I suppose the restlessness and trouble staying on track has been there for a while, even if the getting up during meetings is more recent.
When you think back to your school days and even now, would you say the main struggle has been more about staying focused and organized, or more about the restlessness and difficulty sitting still?

I think it's really been a mix of both, to be honest. I mean, the restlessness is definitely what's bothering me the most right now with the meetings, but the focus and organization part has always been a struggle too. Like I said about my desk in school being a mess and forgetting my homework... that kind of stuff still happens. I still have trouble keeping my workspace organized and I definitely get sidetracked easily. So I wouldn't say one is necessarily worse than the other, they just kind of show up in different ways depending on what I'm doing.

When you were in school, aside from the restlessness and trouble sitting still, would you say you had significant problems with things like impulsivity — like blurting things out, interrupting others, or acting without thinking — or was the main issue more about losing focus and getting distracted?

I don't really remember having a lot of problems with blurting things out or acting without thinking, to be honest. I mean, my teachers did say I talked out of turn sometimes, but I wouldn't say it was a major issue. The main thing was definitely just losing focus, getting distracted, and having a messy desk. I don't recall being super impulsive or anything like that.

You mentioned these focus and organization problems going back to elementary school — but when you think about your very early childhood, like before you started school, do you remember your parents or caregivers mentioning that you had trouble sitting still, paying attention, or following instructions?

Honestly, I don't really remember much from before I started kindergarten, and my parents haven't really said anything about me having trouble back then. Like I mentioned a minute ago, the earliest I can really point to is elementary school. I know for a fact it started way before high school because of those report cards where my teachers wrote that I was bright but rushed through everything. And, you know, the talking out of turn, forgetting my homework, and having my desk stuffed with all those half-finished papers. So I know it goes back at least that far, but as for my very early childhood before school, I'm just not really sure.

Besides school and work, have you noticed these focus and organization problems showing up in other areas of your life — like at home with personal tasks, in your relationships, or in hobbies and activities you do on your own time?

Not really, no. I mean... I haven't really noticed it being much of an issue at home or in my relationships. I guess when I'm on my own time, I'm just doing what I want to do, so I don't really have to force myself to focus the same way I do at the office. My apartment is fine, and with my hobbies... I don't know, I just kind of do what I enjoy, so I don't really get sidetracked. So, yeah, I'd say it's pretty much just work and, you know, back when I was in school, where it really shows up.

When you're at home in the evenings or on weekends, do you find it difficult to keep your personal space organized, or do you struggle to stick with tasks like paying bills, doing laundry, or following through on things you've planned to do for yourself?

Um, no, not really. Like I was just saying, my place is fine. I don't really have an issue keeping things organized or getting my laundry done. And with bills... I mean, I mostly just handle them when they come in, or they're on autopay. I don't really find myself putting that stuff off or struggling to get it done when I'm off the clock. It's really just at work where I feel like I have a hard time keeping on top of things.

When you're doing something you really enjoy at home — like a hobby or an activity you're genuinely interested in — can you sit down and focus on it for a long period without getting up or getting distracted, or do you still find yourself restless and jumping around even when it's something you actually want to be doing?

No, I can usually focus just fine when it's something I want to do. If I'm working on a hobby or something I'm really interested in, I can sit there for hours without any problem. I don't really get restless or feel the need to jump around when it's my own stuff. Like I said, the distraction and the restlessness... it really only happens when I'm at work and have to force myself to do things I'm not that engaged with.

When you were in elementary school and your teachers noted that you rushed through your work and had trouble focusing, were you able to focus well on things you actually enjoyed doing at that time — like playing games, reading comics, or activities you were interested in?

Yeah, from what I remember, it was pretty much the same back then. If I was playing a video game or doing something I actually liked, I could pay attention for a long time. It was really just the schoolwork—like worksheets or reading assignments I didn't care about—where I'd speed through it and make mistakes just to get it over with. But for fun stuff, I didn't have any trouble focusing at all.

When you were in school, did your teachers or parents ever suggest you might have ADHD or attention problems, or did anyone ever recommend that you get evaluated by a doctor for these kinds of issues?

No, I don't think anyone ever brought that up. I mean, my teachers definitely noticed I was rushing and they'd tell my parents I needed to slow down and check my work, but nobody ever suggested it was an actual medical issue or that I needed to see a doctor for it. I think everyone just assumed I was being careless because I didn't want to do the assignments.

You mentioned your apartment is organized and you handle bills fine, but I want to ask more specifically: when you're at work on tasks that aren't meetings — like reading emails, writing reports, or working through documents — do you find yourself getting distracted or having trouble staying focused on those things too, or is it really just the sitting-still part during meetings that's the main problem?

It happens with that stuff too, actually. It's not just the sitting still part. Like, if I'm in one of our longer strategy meetings, or if I'm sitting at my desk trying to read through a client brief... I usually start out focused. But then after a few minutes, I'll suddenly realize I've just been staring at the exact same slide, or the same paragraph, and I have absolutely no idea what the last point even was. I just kind of zone out while looking right at it, so I end up having to go back and reread things a lot.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a long-standing pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity dating back to elementary school (age 6–7+), with symptoms persisting into adulthood. Key diagnostic features include: (1) childhood onset with teacher-documented inattention ('rushed through work,' 'talked out of turn,' 'forgot homework,' disorganized desk); (2) persistent difficulty sustaining attention in non-preferred tasks at work (zoning out during meetings and while reading briefs); (3) hyperactivity manifesting as inability to remain seated in meetings and restlessness; (4) symptoms present across multiple settings (school historically, work currently); (5) functional impairment in occupational/academic contexts; (6) normal functioning in preferred activities and self-directed tasks (hobbies, personal organization). The pattern is consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive-hyperactive type, which manifests primarily in externally structured, lower-interest environments. F90.9 (Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, unspecified) is the appropriate diagnosis given the mixed presentation and lack of specific subtype clarification in the interview.
